title: K-Means Clustering
summary:
K-means splits points into **K clusters** by repeating two steps with `K` centroids (think of K magnets pulling points toward their centre of gravity):

1. **Assign** every point to its nearest centroid (Euclidean).
2. **Update** every centroid to the mean of its points.

Repeat until the assignments stop changing (or a max iteration count). If an assignment pass changes nothing, the means are the same, so the algorithm is at a fixed point. The result is *hard* clustering: each point belongs to one cluster.

It minimises **inertia** (within-cluster sum of squares) `J = sum |x - mu_k|^2`. Neither step can increase `J`, so it converges, but only to a **local** optimum. Hence: seed with `k-means++` and run several restarts; re-seed an empty cluster.

**Choosing K:** inertia always falls as K grows (K = n gives 0), so look for the **elbow**, or use the **silhouette** `s = (b - a) / max(a, b)` (a = mean distance to own cluster, b = to the nearest other cluster), and finally ask what K the product needs.

**Assumptions:** numeric features on comparable scales (standardize), roughly round clusters of similar size and density. It struggles with outliers, rings, and elongated shapes (consider DBSCAN or Gaussian mixtures). Cost is `O(n K d t)`.

In systems, k-means builds the cells of [IVF indexes](#/sd/f/similarity-search) and groups [embeddings](#/sd/f/item-embedding).

drills.q: 1-D points: 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12. Initial centroids c1 = 1 and c2 = 2. After the first assignment (each point to the nearest centroid; ties are none here) and update step, what is the new c2?
Continue the previous example for one more iteration with centroids c1 = 1 and c2 = 7.6 until it converges. What is the final inertia (sum of squared distances to the final centroids)?
drills.explain: Second assignment: 1, 2, 3 -> c1 (mean 2); 10, 11, 12 -> c2 (mean 11). The next pass changes nothing. Inertia = (1+0+1) + (1+0+1) = 4.

drills.q: Inertia for K = 1..6 on a customer dataset is 1000, 400, 200, 180, 170, 165. A colleague proposes K = 6 because it has the lowest inertia. What is the better reasoning?
options: K = 6 is right: lower inertia always means a better model
K = 1 is right because it is the simplest
K = 3 is the elbow: going from 3 to 4 only gains 20 while 2 to 3 gained 200; confirm with silhouette and the business need
Inertia cannot be compared across K, so pick K at random
drills.explain: Inertia decreases monotonically with K and reaches 0 at K = n, so the minimum is meaningless. The elbow marks where extra clusters stop paying off; check with silhouette and what the segments are used for.

drills.q: You cluster customers on two features: annual income (0 to 200,000 dollars) and age (18 to 80). The clusters turn out to be basically income bands. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Euclidean distance is dominated by the larger-scale feature; standardize features before clustering
K-means ignores features with larger values; use cosine
K is too small; double it
Age is categorical so k-means cannot use it
drills.explain: A difference of 10,000 in income swamps a difference of 30 in age. Standardizing (z-scores) puts the features on comparable scale. Raising K does not change the dominance.

drills.q: Put one k-means run in order.
items: Choose K and seed the centroids (k-means++)
Assign every point to its nearest centroid
Recompute each centroid as the mean of its points
Stop when assignments no longer change or a max iteration is reached
drills.explain: Assignment and update alternate until a fixed point. Empty clusters need a fresh centroid, otherwise a centroid has no mean to move to.

drills.q: A point has mean distance a = 2 to the other points in its own cluster and mean distance b = 6 to the points of the nearest other cluster. What is its silhouette value, to two decimals?
drills.explain: s = (b - a) / max(a, b) = (6 - 2) / 6 = 0.667. Near 1 means well matched to its own cluster; near 0 means on the border; negative means probably in the wrong cluster.
